newsitem.title: USA: Author pins 1871 Chicago fire on "Peg Leg" Sullivan.
newsitem.headline: Author pins 1871 Chicago fire on "Peg Leg" Sullivan.

text.p: Contrary to the findings of an official board shortly after the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, the fire was probably started by a neighbour of the infamous Mrs. O'Leary, whose cow was blamed for the devastating blaze.

Chicago lawyer and historian Dick Bales, whose research will be published in the Illinois Historical Journal, said Tuesday the fire began in O'Leary's barn, but the often-told tale blaming the poor Irish immigrant and her latern-kicking cow was flawed.
The fire killed 250 people and left the city in ashes, causing nearly $200 million damage.

Bales put the blame on Daniel "Peg Leg" Sullivan, who lived across DeKoven Street from Catherine O'Leary, saying he may have ignited the Oct. 8 blaze by dropping a match or an ash from his pipe inside Mrs. O'Leary's barn.
Mrs. O'Leary "was a scapegoat for the older, native-born men who served on the inquiry into the fire," Bales said.

He said the original inquiry ignored inconsistencies in Sullivan's story, who testified he was across the street when he spotted the cow kick the lantern, dashed across to save a calf, then awakened O'Leary in her bed.

Bales said he doubted Sullivan's wooden leg would have permitted such haste, but it was his meticulous reconstruction of DeKoven Street and review of the testimony at the inquiry that pointed to Sullivan as the culprit.

A scale model of the street showed Sullivan's view of the barn from his porch was blocked by another home that was destroyed in the fire. Sullivan also gave sharply conflicting statements about where the fire actually started, Bales said.
